fact: The word myth comes from the ancient Greek word "mythos," which simply meant "story" or "speech." The Greeks used myths to explain mysterious things like thunder, seasons, and why the sun moved across the sky. Today we use it for stories that aren't quite true, but they often teach us something important anyway.

Did you know "gym" is short for gymnasium, which comes from ancient Greece? Greek athletes used to exercise completely naked, and the word comes from "gymnos" meaning naked! Don't worry though, nowadays we definitely wear clothes to PE. The Greeks thought physical fitness was just as important as learning maths and reading.

The word pyramid comes from the ancient Greek word "pyramis", which might have come from the Egyptian word for wheat cake! Some think the Greeks named these massive stone structures after pointy cakes because of their triangular shape. Imagine comparing one of the world's greatest wonders to a snack!

Mystery comes from the ancient Greek word "mysterion," which meant a secret religious ceremony. Only special people were allowed to know what happened! The word is related to "myein," meaning to close your eyes or mouth — because you had to keep these secrets hidden. Pretty mysterious, right?

Did you know "symbol" comes from an ancient Greek tradition? When friends parted ways, they'd break a stick or coin in half. Each person kept one piece. When they met again, they'd fit the pieces together to prove their friendship! That's why symbols represent something meaningful.

Rhythm is one of the trickiest words to spell because it has no ordinary vowels in the middle — just Y and H! It comes from a Greek word meaning "flow," like waves moving in the sea. Remember: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move. That silly sentence might help you never forget those tricky letters again!

Here's a fun fact about the word typical! It comes from the Greek word "typos" which meant a mark or impression, like when you stamp something into clay. So when we say something is typical, we're saying it fits the pattern or matches the usual stamp of how things are. Cool, right?

Did you know "system" comes from an ancient Greek word meaning "to stand together"? The Greeks noticed how parts of things work as a team — like your body's organs or the planets in space. When something is a system, all its pieces are standing together to make it work!

Did you know crystal comes from the ancient Greek word for ice? People long ago thought clear quartz was ice frozen so hard it would never melt! The Greeks called it "krustallos" which means icy cold. Now we use crystal for anything beautifully clear and sparkly, from chandeliers to snowflakes.

Did you know gymnast comes from the ancient Greek word "gymnos" meaning naked? That's because Greek athletes used to train and compete without clothes! They thought it helped them move freely. Don't worry though — modern gymnasts wear leotards and shorts. The Greeks also gave us gymnasium, which literally meant "a place to train naked"!

Did you know "division" comes from a Latin word meaning "to force apart"? The Romans used it when they split things into separate pieces. That's why we use it in maths when we share numbers out, and why it can also mean when people disagree and get pulled in different directions!

Did you know "invasion" comes from a Latin word meaning "to go into"? The Romans used it when their armies marched into new territories. The "vas" part is related to "go" or "walk" – so an invasion is literally when someone goes into a place where they're not welcome!

Did you know "confusion" comes from Latin words meaning "to pour together"? Imagine pouring different coloured paints into one pot — everything mixes up and you can't tell them apart anymore! That's exactly how the Romans thought about confusion: like lots of thoughts getting poured together in your mind until nothing makes sense.

Did you know that "decision" comes from a Latin word meaning "to cut off"? When you make a decision, you're cutting away all the other choices! Ancient Romans imagined it like using scissors — snip! — to remove everything except the one path you pick. Pretty cool way to think about choosing, right?

Did you know "invention" comes from a Latin word meaning "to come upon" or "to find"? The Romans used it when someone discovered something new. I love that! It's like inventors are explorers who stumble upon brilliant ideas hiding in their imagination. Every invention starts with someone finding a clever solution to a problem.

Did you know "injection" comes from Latin words meaning "to throw in"? Doctors literally throw medicine into your body! The "ject" part appears in lots of words: eject means throw out, project means throw forward, and reject means throw back. Once you spot it, you'll see it everywhere!

Here's a fun fact about completion! It comes from the Latin word "complere," which means "to fill up." Imagine pouring water into a glass until it's totally full — that's the idea behind completion. When you complete something, you're filling it up to the very end, leaving nothing empty or unfinished!

Did you know "discussion" comes from a Latin word meaning "to shake apart"? Ancient Romans imagined that when you discuss something, you're breaking down ideas into smaller pieces to examine them properly. So next time you have a discussion in class, you're literally shaking ideas apart to understand them better!

Did you know "permission" comes from a Latin word meaning "to let go through"? Imagine a gatekeeper stepping aside to let you pass! When you ask for permission, you're really asking someone to let you through to do something. That's why we say someone "gives" you permission.

Did you know "expression" comes from a Latin word meaning "to press out"? Imagine squeezing juice from an orange — that's the idea! When you express yourself, you're pressing your thoughts and feelings out into the world through words, art, or even the look on your face. Pretty cool, right?

Did you know "poisonous" comes from the Latin word "potio," which meant a drink or potion? In medieval times, people worried about deadly drinks, so "potion" became linked with poison. That's why we spell it with "oi" — it remembers those dangerous drinkable potions from long ago!

Did you know 'dangerous' comes from an old word meaning 'in someone's power'? In medieval times, if you were in danger, you were literally under someone else's control — pretty scary! The 'ous' ending just means 'full of', so dangerous means full of that threatening power. Makes sense, doesn't it?

Did you know "famous" comes from the Latin word "fama," which meant rumour or reputation? In ancient Rome, if people were talking about you everywhere, you had fama! The word travelled through French before reaching English. So being famous literally means everyone's heard your name being passed around!

Did you know "enormous" comes from a Latin word meaning "out of the normal pattern"? It's made from "e" (out of) and "norma" (a carpenter's square for measuring). So when something is enormous, it's literally gone beyond the normal measurements! Ancient Romans would have been amazed by how we use it today.

Here's a fun fact about generous! It comes from the Latin word "genus" meaning "birth" or "family." Long ago, people from noble families were expected to be kind and give freely to others. So being generous meant acting like you came from a good family. Now anyone can be generous by sharing what they have!

Did you know "courageous" comes from the French word "coeur", which means heart? People used to believe that bravery lived inside your heart! So when you're being courageous, you're acting "with heart". Next time you do something brave, remember you're letting your heart lead the way!

Here's a fun one! Mischievous comes from an old French word meaning "to come to a bad end." But over time, it softened to mean playful naughtiness rather than anything truly terrible. So when you're being mischievous, you're just being a little bit cheeky, not actually wicked!

Did you know "marvellous" comes from the Latin word "mirabilis," which means "wonderful to behold"? It's related to "miracle"! When something is truly marvellous, it makes you stop and stare in amazement. The double L in the middle can be tricky to remember, but think of it as doubling the wonder!

Did you know "gorgeous" comes from an old French word meaning "elegant" or "fashionable"? Back in medieval times, it described fancy clothing and jewellery that made people look stunning. Over time, we started using it for anything beautiful – sunsets, cakes, even your best friend's new trainers!

Did you know "hideous" comes from an old French word meaning "fear" or "dread"? In medieval times, people used it to describe things that made them shiver with fright. So when something looks absolutely hideous, you're basically saying it's scary-looking! The spelling might seem odd, but that "eous" ending is quite common in words borrowed from French.
